items.question: Why do you think the concept of an intelligence explosion is misleading?
items.object: The concept of an intelligence explosion
items.answer: I think it's not a very useful concept. It's kind of like calling the Industrial Revolution a horsepower explosion. Sure, during the Industrial Revolution, we saw this drastic acceleration in raw physical power, but there are many other things that were maybe equally important in explaining the acceleration of growth and technological change that we saw during the Industrial Revolution.
quotes: I think it's not a very useful concept. It's kind of like calling the Industrial Revolution a horsepower explosion. Sure, during the Industrial Revolution, we saw this drastic acceleration in raw physical power, but there are many other things that were maybe equally important in explaining the acceleration of growth and technological change that we saw during the Industrial Revolution.

rubrics.text: The response compares the term “intelligence explosion” to describing the Industrial Revolution as a “horsepower explosion.”
The response states that factors other than increased physical power may have been equally important in explaining the Industrial Revolution’s acceleration of economic growth.

items.question: How do you think the Industrial Revolution helps us understand the economic transformation that AI could bring?
items.object: The Industrial Revolution as an analogy for AI-driven economic transformation
items.answer: So I think in the case of the Industrial Revolution, it was a bunch of these complementary changes to many different sectors in the economy. So you had agriculture, you had transportation, you had law and finance, you had urbanization and moving from rural areas into cities. There were just many different innovations that happened simultaneously that gave rise to this change in the way of economically organizing our society. It wasn't just that we had more horsepower. I mean, that was part of it, but that's not the kind of central thing to focus on when thinking about the Industrial Revolution. And I think similarly, for the development of AI, sure, we'll get a lot of very smart AI systems, but that will be one part among very many different moving parts that explain why we expect to get this transition and this acceleration in growth and technological change.
quotes: So I think in the case of the Industrial Revolution, it was a bunch of these complementary changes to many different sectors in the economy. So you had agriculture, you had transportation, you had law and finance, you had urbanization and moving from rural areas into cities. There were just many different innovations that happened simultaneously that gave rise to this change in the way of economically organizing our society.
It wasn't just that we had more horsepower. I mean, that was part of it, but that's not the kind of central thing to focus on when thinking about the Industrial Revolution.

And I think similarly, for the development of AI, sure, we'll get a lot of very smart AI systems, but that will be one part among very many different moving parts that explain why we expect to get this transition and this acceleration in growth and technological change.

The response states that increasingly capable AI systems are only one of multiple factors expected to drive the economic transformation associated with AI.

items.question: How do you think about when AI will become a drop-in remote worker replacement?
items.object: AI as a drop-in remote worker replacement
items.answer: I'm a little bit more bullish. I mean, it depends what you mean by “drop-in remote worker” and whether it's able to do literally everything that can be done remotely, or do most things.
quotes: I'm a little bit more bullish. I mean, it depends what you mean by “drop-in remote worker” and whether it's able to do literally everything that can be done remotely, or do most things.

rubrics.text: The response distinguishes AI replacement of remote workers on every remotely performable task from replacement on most such tasks as different meanings of a “drop-in remote worker replacement.”

items.question: How do you use past AI capability advances and compute scaling to assess how far we are from automating remote work?
items.object: Compute scaling and the remaining capabilities needed to automate remote work
items.answer: I think what Ege is referring to is, if you look at the past 10 years of AI progress, we've gone through about nine or 10 orders of magnitude of compute, and we got various capabilities that were unlocked. So in the early period, people were solving gameplay on specific games, on very complex games. And that happened from 2015 to 2020, Go and Chess and Dota and other games. And then you had maybe sophisticated language capabilities that were unlocked with these large language models, and maybe advanced abstract reasoning and coding and maybe math. That was maybe another big capability that got unlocked. And so maybe there are a couple of these big unlocks that happened over the past 10 years, but that happened on the order of once every three years or so, or maybe one every three orders of magnitude of compute scaling. And then you might ask the question, “How many more such competencies might we need to unlock in order to be able to have an AI system that can match the capabilities of humans across the board?” Maybe specifically just on remote work tasks. And so then you might ask, well, maybe you need kind of coherence over very long horizons, or you need agency and autonomy, or maybe you need full multimodal understanding, just like a human would. And then you ask the question, “Okay, how long might that take?” And so you can think about, well, just in terms of calendar years, the previous unlocks took about—you get one every three years or so. But of course, that previous period coincided with this rapid scale-up of the amount of compute that we use for training. So we went through maybe 9 or 10 orders of magnitude since AlexNet compared to the biggest models we have today. And we're getting to a level where it's becoming harder and harder to scale up compute. And we've done some extrapolations and some analysis looking at specific constraints, like energy or GPU production. And based on that, it looks like we might have maybe three or four orders of magnitude of scaling left. And then you're really spending a pretty sizable fraction or a non-trivial fraction of world output on just building up data centers, energy infrastructure, fabs, and so on.

items.question: Why do you think the ability to perform simple computer tasks like booking a flight does not establish full agentic computer use?
items.object: Composing simple computer tasks into full agentic computer use
items.answer: I mean, sure, but they are not disconnected tasks. That's like saying everything you do in the world is just like you just move parts of your body, and then you move your mouth and your tongue, and then you roll your head. Yeah, individually those things are simple, but then how do you put them together, right?

items.question: What convinced you that Ege Erdil should work on economic questions at Epoch?
items.object: Ege Erdil’s knowledge of economics and suitability for Epoch
items.answer: We connected on a Discord for Metaculus, which is this forecasting platform. And I was a graduate student at Cambridge at the time doing research in economics. And I was having conversations with my peers there. And I was occasionally having conversations with Ege. And I was like, “This guy knows a lot more about economics”. And at the time he was a computer science undergrad in Ankara. And he knows more about economics and about these big trends in economic growth and economic history than almost any of my peers at the university. And so, like, what the hell is up with that? And then we started having frequent collaborations and ended up hiring Ege for Epoch because it clearly makes sense for him to work on these types of questions.

items.question: Why did you see starting Epoch as a better way to pursue the research you were excited about?
items.answer: So I was at MIT doing more research, and I was pretty unhappy with the bureaucracy there where it was very hard for me to scale projects up, hire people. And I was pretty excited about a bunch of work that my PI wasn't excited about because it's maybe hard to publish or it doesn't confer the same prestige. And so I was chatting with Jaime Sevilla, one of the co-founders, and we just collaborated on projects and then thought we should just start our own org, because we can just hire people and work on the projects we were excited about.

items.question: What opportunity did you see in founding Epoch to study the future of AI?
items.answer: It was more like we can make a bunch of progress because clearly academia and industry is kind of dropping the ball on a bunch of important questions that academia is unable to publish interesting papers on. Industry is not really focused on producing useful insights. And so it seemed very good for us to just do that. And also the timing was very good. So we started just before ChatGPT and we wanted to have much more grounded discussions of the future of AI. And I was frustrated with the quality of discussion that was happening on the internet about the future of AI. And to some extent or to a very large extent, I still am. And that's a large part of what motivates me to do this. It's just born out of frustration with bad thinking and arguments about where AI is going to go.

items.question: Why do you see mathematics as a useful sandbox for testing AI research ability?
items.object: Mathematics as a benchmark for research reasoning
items.answer:
I think math is quite unique in the sense that it's one of the few domains of science where you have arguments, precise analytical arguments that span many pages. In extreme cases it might span hundreds of pages to prove some result. And in many cases you can do this verification, you can check whether the answer is correct. And so that's why it's this nice sandbox for testing the ability to do research and R&D relevant reasoning over very long horizons, and still being able to do automatic verification. You don't have to get a peer reviewer in to be able to tell whether this work is any good. And so that's why I think math is really nice and so you can test this longer-horizon ability. Yeah, so we are really trying to capture modern mathematical understanding across many, many domains and branches of math.

And even some that are fairly obscure where only maybe 10 people in the world would know how to solve some of these problems. You know, we want to be able to test for the ability to do this kind of creative reasoning, to connect disparate ideas in the literature and figure out how to use them in a way that enables you to solve this problem. And I think we've seen less of that in AI so far, where we haven't seen as much progress on combining ideas creatively and coming up with this kind of very creative flashes of insight that make scientific progress. So that is something that I'm excited to try to test for and have a really good benchmark for at least some dimension of that.

items.question: Why do you think AI's economic value could grow faster than its measured performance?
items.object: Economic returns to AI capability improvements
items.answer:
There are some reasons to think that there are faster than linear gains that you might sometimes see when increasing compute exponentially. And one reason is that there are larger gains in terms of the value of having certain AI capabilities around human-level performance. And so that's because, for example, having a self-driving car that is 10% worse than humans is not worth, you know, it's not worth 10% less than having a self-driving car that matches human performance. And so sometimes in some more important metric like the value that this system generates, you might get faster than linear gains, at least on some portions of this curve, such as maybe around human-level performance.

And then other reasons for maybe expecting things to increase faster than linearly is that there are increasing returns in AI or there are economies of scale. So for instance, for earlier systems like early language models like BERT or GPT-2, it just wasn't worth building a lot of really great tooling like what you have in ChatGPT with a code interpreter and what Claude has with artifacts and things like this because you just didn't have many users, and so spending that fixed cost didn't allow you to amortize this over a large number of users. And the same is true for the kind of cost that you incur during training. Just this one-time cost that you can amortize over the users that you have. And, you know, earlier on for these very small systems, it didn't make sense to spend all that much on those fixed costs because you couldn't amortize it over many users. You didn't have many users who were willing to pay for it. But now, you start to get more and more users as you improve the performance of these systems. And so this starts this flywheel where it starts to make sense to spend a lot more money on the training, on post-training, on building a really great way of interacting with these models, which before didn't quite make sense.

items.question: How do you think uncertainty about full labor automation should affect investment in AI scaling?
items.object: The information value of AI scale-ups
items.answer:
So one thing is that even if you're uncertain about whether you can fully substitute for human labor, you might get partial automation. And that partial automation is itself quite valuable. And so already, OpenAI and others are making billions of dollars in revenue. If they're able to automate some fraction, not quite 100% but some fraction short of that, I think that is still going to be worth maybe on the order of trillions of dollars. And so even without being certain that you're able to fully automate everything, it's worth doing just on an expected value calculation. The other thing is that it is also extremely valuable to resolve this uncertainty. There's a lot of value of information. And you get a lot of information by doing your next scale-up and expanding your infrastructure for handling that scale-up. And so resolving this uncertainty soon is going to be really valuable because maybe doing the next training run tells you that, oh, actually this looks a lot easier than people expected. And if that's the case, then it would be extremely valuable to know because that would enable us to get to this goal of having AI that is able to be substituted for human labor much more quickly, which would be extremely valuable.

And so this value of information consideration itself is also really quite useful.

items.question: How do you judge the weight investors place on new AI product demonstrations?
items.object: AI demonstrations versus scaling research as investment evidence
items.answer:
I think accounts of the CEOs of some of these hyperscalers suggest that yes, these demonstrations have been really quite important. I think maybe there's too much paying attention to some of these demonstrations and maybe not enough to just purely looking at the body of research that has validated some of these ideas around scaling. So, I think there's maybe too much attention being paid to the details of the capabilities of these systems that are being launched and precisely how many customers they're able to serve and how much revenue they're able to generate. Like I think the real prize here is being able to build a system that flexibly substitutes for human labor. And we should keep our eye on this prize and not get too distracted by whether we're able to package this nice business enterprise product.

And now, maybe this gives us some insight into how successful deep learning is, but I think the research that we have, the papers on scaling laws and other things, are maybe more important for giving us an indication about how good these systems are that we're currently building and the techniques that we have for building them.

items.question: Why do you favor expanding AI chip infrastructure before AI generates large revenues?
items.object: Advance investment in AI chip infrastructure
items.answer:
I think the more efficient allocation would probably involve a lot more spending and a lot more production of chips and related infrastructure right now. Like I expect that we will have these extremely large training runs and have a lot of compute that is going to be needed, and it is inefficient for that scaling to happen exactly when you need it.

You ideally want to scale this up beforehand because there are premiums that you otherwise have to pay where if you very suddenly want to expand your chip production then you have to pay this large premium on making that happen. The more efficient way of doing this would be to more smoothly ramp up production of chips and other capital stock like the energy infrastructure and the lithography machines and other things. So I think in order to avoid this large adjustment cost it makes more sense to do this initial expanded scaling even well in advance of when AI generates a lot of value. And that's because you want to avoid—it's not possible to perfectly time this. You have to prepare your supply chain ahead of time. An analogy for this is something like space colonization. In order to achieve very successful space colonization you might want to get really good at landing on the moon or something like that. Not because you care about landing on the moon but because it helps you flex those muscles.

And so I think that the more efficient thing we could be doing is in fact expand this computer-related capital stock and do these training runs to flex our muscles on being able to have the supply chain running as well as learn a lot about how to do this expansion, how to do these large training runs, and how to provide the energy and all the things that we need to support that.

items.question: What limits do you see to improving AI performance by scaling inference compute?
items.answer:
I think this intuition that there's a limit to the value of scaling inference compute is quite accurate. Then we do see this in examples for math and someone at Scale AI had reproduced some of the inference scaling laws that OpenAI showed where there was this plateauing. Given infinite time it's just not going to—there's some point at which it plateaus such that, even though it might be increasing, it's not going to get you all the way there. It's going to get really expensive and maybe not give you much in terms of improvement. I think part of this is because for some of these tasks we don't have perfect verification. So if you had some oracle that tells you whether the answer's correct then you can just scale up the number of samples to extremely large numbers and you can continue getting some increments in performance, but without that I think it becomes a lot harder and you start to hit these diminishing returns.

And so in this paper—yeah, we wrote something about this at Epoch and we had done some estimates about the span of this trade-off and we summarized some evidence and then estimated that you could get maybe two orders of magnitude of equivalence in training compute. So you could scale up your inference by some large amount and that gives you maybe at most two orders of magnitude of training-compute equivalent.

items.question: How do you think AI developers should divide spending between training and inference compute?
items.object: Allocation between training and inference compute
items.answer: I think the spending on inference compute is too little such that it makes sense to spend more on inference compute. There's a related blog post that we wrote recently where we made this point that the optimal amount of inference compute spending should be roughly half or roughly equivalent to the amount of training compute you're spending. It depends on precisely the class slope of the trade-off, but the basic intuition is that if you spend 99% of your budget on training compute and 1% on inference compute, you can double the amount of inference compute spending very cheaply and get a pretty substantial performance improvement. And the doubling is very cheap because it's only 1%, right? And so it doesn't make sense for this allocation to be very lopsided because then there's a reallocation you can make that keeps your overall budget the same but gives you better performance or allows you to achieve the same amount of performance but with a smaller compute budget. And so we made this point that you should expect inference and training compute spending to be on the same order because of this ability to trade these two things off against each other.
quotes: I think the spending on inference compute is too little such that it makes sense to spend more on inference compute. items.question: What distinction in algorithmic progress matters to your assessment of automated AI research?
items.object: Cost reduction versus frontier expansion in algorithmic progress
items.answer:
I think we've seen progress in terms of algorithmic improvements of broadly two types.

So, one has been of the type of expanding the range of capabilities that models can do, and just making them better at pushing out the boundaries of what models can do. And the other type of algorithmic innovation has been reducing the cost of achieving already attained levels of capabilities. So, this would be things like distillation where you take a large model and distill it by generating synthetic data and training a smaller model to make that smaller model really quite capable and attain the existing capabilities. And so we've seen progress of both types, but maybe it's easier to achieve algorithmic progress that enables you to attain already attained levels of capabilities. And so it's a kind of make it easier to imitate GPT-4. And if it's the case that algorithmic innovations have mostly been making it possible to get the abilities of these larger models more cheaply, then having a lot of automated R&D might not actually expand the set of capabilities you can. And so there's one way in which it does, which is that if you make the model cheaper and smaller you can run more inference and then you can amplify your model and you can get some boost using this inference scaling.

But I think the argument that automating R&D results in this explosion of capabilities looks a lot weaker if algorithmic progress has been mostly of the sort that reduces the cost of achieving already attained capabilities. And then there's this other notion of algorithmic progress which just expands what you can do. And I think if that is something that we can automate doing, we can automate the R&D process that expands what these systems are able to do, then I think the argument that we get this feedback loop that results in accelerating progress looks slightly stronger.

items.question: Why would you be concerned if AI laboratories found automated research more valuable than serving external users?
items.object: AI laboratories keeping automated research internal
items.answer:
If it turns out that automating R&D works really well and we get much better systems by spending our compute budgets on AI systems working on improving AI research and producing innovations.

You know, OpenAI and other labs might decide that that's the best use of their compute budgets. So, they should just spend their resources on running these systems internally rather than serving them to others because it's really valuable for them to do this. And so, maybe you don't see a lot of automation happen if the returns to the software R&D and this flywheel is possible such that it makes sense for these labs to spend a lot of their compute budgets. That could be a pretty dangerous situation, would be my guess. If it turns out that automating software R&D is so valuable that labs keep it internal, the world might be surprised at what comes out at the end of that process. So, it looks like not a lot is happening perhaps, and then suddenly you have incredibly capable models.

items.question: How do you think geographically distributed training could ease AI's power bottlenecks?
items.object: Geographically distributed training as a response to power bottlenecks
items.answer:
One kind of interesting issue with energy or power is that for training, right now, the way that training usually happens is that a single campus or data center does the training run. And then you can serve this, you can infer the model across many different data centers. And so, the power demands for training are very highly concentrated. And this makes it run into these bottlenecks much more quickly, because there's only so much power you can get in Northern Virginia at a specific data center. And so that's why there's this struggle and companies are figuring out, you know, can we get contracts with solar farms and nuclear power plants and there's this Three Mile Island that is—there's plans for reopening it for powering data centers. One thing you can do is you can geographically distribute your training. And you can distribute your training where you involve a data center in Northern Virginia, a data center in Pennsylvania, and in many other places. And then you can effectively distribute the power that you need in order to train a model and tap into more energy sources. And, you know, in this report about can we scale through 2030, we worked out that yes, indeed you can do this geographic distribution of your training run.

Now, it requires running a lot of fiber optic cables, but that's something AT&T and other people do and, you know, we have fiber optic cable across oceans. And so, running fiber optic cables is certainly something that it's feasible to do. And that already reduces that, gets you more breathing room and enables you to tap into more energy infrastructure. And so, even without building a lot of energy infrastructure, I suspect that you can already do quite a bit of scaling. A model that's 10,000 times greater than GPT-4 that is on trend for 2030, that's about 5 GW or something. In the US, the total installed capacity is about 1,000 GW. This is 0.5%. Quite a lot, but in some sense if it's the most important industrial technology or whatever, then I think this seems well justified.
